title: 1 May and BMS: how the movement marks the day
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Why BMS keeps 17 September, Vishwakarma Jayanti, as its labour day, how May Day began, and what the eight-hour day means in India after the new labour codes.
body:
On 1 May, workers in dozens of countries march, hold meetings and receive a holiday. India has its own early place in that story: the first May Day in India was held in Madras in 1923. Yet Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS), India's largest central trade union organisation, does not treat 1 May as its own festival. This post explains where May Day comes from, why BMS looks to a different day, what the two traditions have in common, and why the eight-hour day that both honour is still a live question for workers in 2026.

## Where May Day comes from

The date has its roots in the struggle for the eight-hour working day in the United States. On 1 May 1886, about 200,000 American workers joined a nationwide strike and demonstrations demanding an eight-hour day, with Chicago a major centre. On 3 May a strike at the McCormick Reaper plant in Chicago turned violent, and on 4 May a rally at Haymarket Square was broken up by police. A bomb exploded among the officers, killing seven police, and police fire then killed several people and wounded about 200. The events became known as the Haymarket affair. In 1889 an international socialist conference declared 1 May a day of labour solidarity to commemorate those events, and the date has since come to be called International Workers' Day.

## May Day in India

The first May Day in India was marked in Madras (now Chennai) on 1 May 1923. Two public meetings were held, one at Marina Beach near the High Court and the other at Thiruvanmiyur Beach. The organiser was the labour leader Malayapuram Singaravelu, who presided at the Marina meeting. The speakers asked for an eight-hour working day, better wages, welfare measures and democratic rights for labourers, and Singaravelu also urged that 1 May be declared a public holiday. At the same meeting he announced the formation of the Labour Kisan Party of Hindustan. The day thus began in India as part of an early labour movement that was entangled with the wider freedom struggle.

## The BMS approach

BMS was founded on 23 July 1955 by Dattopant Thengadi, and from the beginning it set out to build a labour movement on different foundations from the class-conflict tradition that dominated the field at the time. Its motto, shown on its website, calls for the nation to be industrialised, industry to be "labourised" and labour to be nationalised, and it ties the interest of the nation, the industry and the worker together.

On that basis BMS chooses **Vishwakarma Jayanti**, observed on 17 September for uniformity across the country, as its day of labour, and has long asked that it be recognised as a National Labour Day. Vishwakarma is regarded in Indian tradition as the divine craftsman and the patron of artisans and builders. BMS sees in the festival a view of work as a creative, even sacred, act, and of the relationship between worker and employer as that of a family rather than that of opposing classes. BMS's own website records its observance of Labour Day on 17 September, with leaders of its units taking part in programmes.

The argument against 1 May was set out in a piece by a former BMS national president, C. K. Saji Narayanan, in the weekly Organiser. In his account, the Chicago agitation of 1886 was a peaceful strike on 1 May and the violence came on 3 and 4 May; the American labour movement itself later chose to observe its Labour Day in September; and the 1 May observance spread through the efforts of the Communist International, which in his view later put it to political uses. He concludes that the day is a foreign import which does not inspire Indian workers in the way Vishwakarma Jayanti does. These are the views of the author and of BMS, and readers who want the wider historical debate should consult other accounts. The point for this post is simply that BMS's choice of a different day is a matter of philosophy, not indifference to workers' rights.

## What both days share

For all the disagreement about the calendar, the two traditions share more than is sometimes admitted.

- Both honour the **dignity of labour** and ask that the person who produces wealth be treated as a person.
- Both remember that the **eight-hour day** was won by organised effort and not granted as a favour.
- Both insist on **safety and decent conditions** at the place of work.
- Both rest on the experience that **organised effort** gets results where individual complaint does not.

## The eight-hour day in 2026

The eight-hour day is not a closed chapter. Under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which came into effect with the other labour codes on 21 November 2025, the maximum daily working time in factories is reduced from nine hours to eight, but the total window within which the work and breaks may be spread is extended from ten hours to twelve, and the quarterly limit on overtime is raised from 50 hours to 125, with overtime still payable at twice the normal rate. For shops and commercial establishments the position depends largely on State laws, which generally set a weekly limit of 48 hours but differ on daily limits and overtime. It is not yet fully clear how the Code will interact with those State laws.

The same shift is visible in sector-specific law. For beedi and cigar workers, the older Act of 1966 allowed shifts of up to nine hours with a 48-hour weekly cap; the new Code sets the standard day at eight hours, keeps the 48-hour weekly limit, requires overtime at double the wage rate, lowers the qualifying period for annual paid leave from 240 days to 180 days and gives a right to free annual health check-ups. These are real changes and they are worth reading closely. A rule that shortens the working day while lengthening the spread-over may help some workers and hurt others, which is why workers' organisations need to read the detail.

## What remains to be done

Law on paper is only the beginning. A large share of India's workforce is informal, which means no written appointment, no wage slip, no fixed hours and no weekly rest. Home-based and platform workers often have no clear employer at all. The challenge for every labour organisation, whichever day it marks, is to bring those workers inside the protection of the law and into organisations that can speak for them.

## Questions for the day

On any day that honours labour, it is worth asking a few plain questions about the workers around you. Do they have a written contract or appointment letter? Do they receive a wage slip? Do they get a weekly day off, and are extra hours paid at the proper rate? Is there a safe place to work and someone to complain to? If the answer to any of these is no, the festival, whether in May or in September, has work left to do.
